answer:
In the large Phase 3 trial of about 4,800 children aged 5–36 months in Burkina Faso, Kenya, Mali, and Tanzania, R21/Matrix-M reduced clinical malaria substantially during the first year after the initial three-dose series:

75% efficacy when doses were timed before the high-transmission season.
68% efficacy with an age-based schedule in areas with year-round transmission.
Among children aged 5–17 months, average efficacy across sites was 78% over the first year.

A booster dose given about a year later helped maintain protection for at least another 6–12 months. The vaccine was generally well tolerated; fever and injection-site pain were among the most common reactions, and the trial reported no treatment-related deaths. These figures describe protection against clinical malaria in the trial—not complete prevention of infection or a guarantee of the same effect in every setting. [1][2][3]
